summary: This is a page from the Django 5.0 documentation explaining class-based views, which are callables that take a request and return a response and let developers structure views with inheritance and mixins. It covers basic view classes (View, RedirectView, TemplateView), using generic views directly in the URLconf via as_view(), subclassing generic views, supporting extra HTTP methods such as HEAD for a book list API, and asynchronous class-based views. Site navigation, language menus and footer boilerplate are ignored.
one_line: Django 5.0 documentation on class-based views: base view classes, URLconf usage, subclassing, HTTP method handling and async views.
key_facts: A view is a callable which takes a request and returns a response, and Django provides classes that can be used as views.
All views inherit from the View class, which handles linking the view into the URLs, HTTP method dispatching and other common features.
RedirectView provides an HTTP redirect, and TemplateView extends the base class to also render a template.
Any arguments passed to as_view() override attributes set on the class, as in TemplateView.as_view(template_name="about.html").
To subclass TemplateView, the example sets template_name = "about.html" in a class named AboutView inside some_app/views.py.
The as_view() class method provides a function-like entry point to class-based views so they can be used in a URLconf.
In the book library example, BookListView defines a head() method that returns a response with a Last-Modified header in RFC 1123 date format based on the most recent book's publication_date.
A HEAD request to the book list view returns an empty body with the Last-Modified header, so the client can decide whether to download the full object list.
A GET request to the book list view returns an object list using the book_list.html template.
View subclasses may define asynchronous (async def) method handlers, such as an async get() that awaits asyncio.sleep(1) and returns HttpResponse("Hello async world!").
Within a single view class, all user-defined method handlers must be either synchronous (def) or all asynchronous (async def).
An ImproperlyConfigured exception will be raised in as_view() if def and async def declarations are mixed in one view class.
Django automatically detects asynchronous views and runs them in an asynchronous context.
